Best Solo Board Games: 5 Picks for a Quiet Night In

2026-09-23

The best solo board game is not a consolation prize for having no friends. It is a different kind of game. I spent a winter home alone five nights a week, and solo games are what kept me sane through it.

Here is what I found: solo gaming is one of the fastest growing corners of the whole hobby, and some of the highest rated games ever made were built to play alone. Spirit Island sits at an 8.5 on BoardGameGeek. Under Falling Skies and Final Girl both sit at 8.1. These are not throwaways. They are the real thing.

I have played a lot of solo games and kept the five below. They cover every mood and budget, from a $13 wallet game I take on flights to a $65 classic people sink hundreds of hours into. Here is the list, and what I honestly think of each.

What a Solo Game Needs (And What Kills It)

A solo game has three jobs. It must present a puzzle that does not solve itself. It needs a target to chase, a score or a win condition, so you want a second game the moment the first one ends. And it has to set up fast, because the only person cleaning up is you.

Here is the key insight: most games fail this because they were built for a group. A bluffing game becomes a card flip when nobody is across the table. A party game becomes a chore. The best solo games are designed from the ground up for one brain, and they get harder as you get better, not easier.

1. Sprawlopolis. The $13 Wallet Game I Play the Most.

Sprawlopolis is 18 cards and a rule sheet you can read in five minutes. You draw cards to build a city, and three scoring cards decide what that city is worth. You do not get to choose the city you build. You score the same city against three different rules at once, and cracking it is a genuine puzzle.

It is the game I actually play the most. No box, it is a wallet. I have played it on an airplane tray in mild turbulence. It costs $12.99 and runs about 15 minutes. Every game is different because you draw three fresh scoring conditions every time.

Here is the honest part. It is a score attack. There is no story, no characters, no drama. You bring the drama yourself, the urge to beat last game's number. That is exactly what keeps me coming back to a game smaller than my phone.

2. Friday. The Punishing Deck Builder That Teaches.

Friday is a deck builder where you lose. A lot. You play as Friday, the character from Robinson Crusoe, tromping through an island full of pirates and jungle beasts with a deck of fight cards you are constantly trimming and upgrading.

Here is why that matters. A solo game only works if losing makes you want to try again instead of quit. Friday nails this. The rules take ten minutes, games run 25 minutes, and it costs $19.95. I played it five times before I won once, and it never felt unfair, only like I had played badly.

The honest catch: on a bad draw it can feel luck heavy, and it is not the prettiest game on this list. But it is the one that taught me the most about deck building, and it is the best $20 anyone can spend on solo gaming.

3. Final Girl. A Horror Movie in a Box.

Final Girl turns solo gaming into a horror movie. You play the final girl, the last one standing, trying to survive a masked killer working through a film's worth of victims. One player, one killer, dice and a board that fills with panicking civilians.

It covers exactly two things: tension and dread. The killer hunts, you scramble for weapons, and each scenario replays a different movie. The core box is $24.75 and a game runs about 45 minutes. The first time I played I lost before the second phase, and I still felt like I had watched a good horror movie.

The honest part is the appetite. The base box tells one story. The real depth lives in expansions, one per movie, which add up. If you only want a single box for the price, pick one of the cheaper games above. If you like collecting stories, this is your game.

4. Under Falling Skies. Tower Defense With Dice.

Under Falling Skies is dice placement meets tower defense. Alien ships descend in a grid above your city. Each turn you roll dice, assign them to research or ships or your cannon, and try to shoot the fleet down before it reaches the ground.

The trick is the dice decide your options, and they rarely line up with what you want. That tension is the whole game. It runs 30 minutes, costs $29.99, and the campaign mode quietly turns a clever puzzle into a full season. My first play was a panic. By the third, I was second guessing every single die.

The catch: before the campaign opens up, the early rounds can blur together. Push past it. The campaign, where your city grows and your ship levels up between games, is where it earns its place.

5. Spirit Island. The 90 Minute Brain Burner.

Spirit Island is the heavyweight. You are a nature spirit defending your island from colonizers, with unique powers, growing strength, and a ninety minute puzzle that gets harder the better you play. It is the most respected solo game on BoardGameGeek, rated 8.5.

The honest part about the first play: it is a two hour teaching session with yourself. Complexity is rated 4 out of 5, and the rulebook is a commitment. But the payoff is the deepest, most replayable solo experience money can buy, and at $64.99 it is the pick if you want exactly one serious game.

It also needs the right moment. Spirit Island takes space, time, and focus. If you game in 20 minute pockets, skip it. If you have a free evening, it is the best one you can spend on a board game.

Here is the part I did not expect: playing solo games made me better WITH people. I learned the rules cold because I had no one else to lean on. When my group came back, I was the one who knew the game, who could teach it in three minutes instead of fumbling through the manual. The whole game night improved because I practiced alone. And the cheapest game here, Sprawlopolis at $13, is the one I reach for most. Price does not predict how much a game gets played. Depth does.

How to Pick Your First Solo Game

Match the game to the moment. If you want something for a coffee break, Sprawlopolis. If you want to sharpen your card play in 25 minutes, Friday. If you like stories and dread, Final Girl. If you want a real campaign, Under Falling Skies. If you have a free evening and want the deepest puzzle in the hobby, Spirit Island.

The prices climb for a reason, and so does the commitment. Everything from the $13 wallet game up to the $30 dice game will teach you what solo gaming is about. Spirit Island is the destination, not the starting point. Work up to it.

Here is the Shelf Test. Every game on my shelf has to earn its space, and the question is always the same: would this survive ten plays? Sprawlopolis would survive a hundred. Friday survives because losing makes you want to fix it. Spirit Island survives for years. That test, not the price tag, is why this list is what it is.

If you want one solo game to start, do not overthink it. Get Sprawlopolis for $12.99. It fits in a pocket, sets up faster than your coffee, and it is the one I actually play the most.
